passage.title: The Bridge
paras: My father built bridges for a living,
steel ones, over rivers I never saw.
At home he could not mend a sentence;
He showed his love in measurements:
how far, how strong, how much weight
a thing could carry before it broke.
I did not understand the numbers.
Now I cross his bridges in my car
and feel them take my weight without complaint,
and I think, too late and not too late,
this is what he was saying.

passage.title: Section A model: The Bridge
paras: The poet presents a father's love as solid but unspoken. The extended metaphor of bridges runs through the poem: the father could build 'steel ones, over rivers' yet 'could not mend a sentence', so the speaker sees the irony of a man who joined places but not people. 'We spoke across a gap' makes their silence a river of its own. The shift in the final stanza, as the speaker crosses 'his bridges' and feels them take 'my weight without complaint', turns the father's work into his message, and the paradox 'too late and not too late' captures regret and comfort together.

passage.title: Section B model (choose your own pair)
paras: Both poets present memory as something fragile that must be held carefully, but whereas one poem fixes it in a single object, the other lets it drift through repeated images. Zoom in on one word in each poem to show the difference.

passage.title: Section C model
paras: Steinbeck uses the dream of the farm to show how hope sustains the powerless: George's repeated telling becomes almost a ritual, yet its destruction exposes how the Depression left men like Lennie and George with no secure place.
